newsitem.title: UK: FEATURE - Lower for longer, interest rate cycle hits bottom.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Lower for longer, interest rate cycle hits bottom.

text.p: Since the early 1990s interest rates have been running lower as the world dragged itself out of recession, but things are picking up and the cycle is bottoming out, financial analysts say.
Markets are pondering every economic statistic, even the minor ones which usually pass without notice, for clues to future policy.
There are only three uncertainties with interest rate moves.
1) The direction.
2) The magnitude.
3 The timing.

Markets usually know two of the three -- the likely direction and the size of the cut or rise. It is usually only a question of timing. But as the economic cycle comes to an end all three come into question.
Is there just one more cut to come or will it be a rise? Will they just raise rates a bit or slam the economic brakes on hard to squash inflation pressures? When is the move coming?
Hence the current jitters and uncertainty in financial markets, particularly stock markets where prices have hit successive record levels of late.

The problem is worse this time because, while it is clear that the interest rate cycle is close to the bottom as some strong growth numbers come through, background inflation pressure is extremely light.
In past economic cycles inflation has fed through alongside economic growth and it was clear that the authorities would err on the side of raising rates quickly.
But this time even when rates do start to climb there will be no need for aggressive tightening because of the favourable inflation backdrop. Rates will remain lower for longer.
"There are structural factors that will keep inflation low," said Nick Stamenkovic, economist at DKB International.

"There is continued intense competition from the Far East and Asia as they export low cost, high quality goods. That is unlikely to change and Western companies have to keep prices low to maintain their competitive edge."
CONSUMER FACTORS
As wage rises are kept low, consumers remain insecure about jobs and retailers will be unable to boost margins because consumers are extremely price conscious.
On top of this, Central Banks are more determined to control inflation this time round, remembering only too clearly what happened in the aftermath of the 1980s boom.
In Europe, the run-up to European Monetary Union (EMU) means fiscal policy has to be kept extremely tight to meet the criteria. This will keep both growth and inflation low.

The main doubt over future interest rate moves surrounds the United States, Japan, Germany, Britain and Canada, with the outlook somewhat clearer for the rest of the Group of Ten (G10) industrialised nations.
UNITED STATES

Structural forces for lower inflation are closer to being played out in the U.S. and, with the economy further through the economic cycle without an output gap -- what the economy is producing compared what what it could potentially produce -- there is more reason to think the Federal Reserve will tighten than cut again.

"I'm inclined to wonder whether it's easy for the Fed to build a case to tighten this year given that they didn't go in July and August when the backdrop was much less ambiguous," said Robin Marshall, chief economist at Chase Investment Bank.
"But that doesn't pre-judge the fact that you might get a tightening in the first half of next year."
JAPAN

The Tankan -- the Bank of Japan's quarterly business survey -- at the end of November will be crucial for the interest rate outlook but a one-off hike in Japanese rates could come at any time, analysts said.

While rates are at an historic low of just 0.5 percent, a rise next spring would make the most sense and even then, the need to tighten fiscal policy and low inflation should keep rates low for some time.
GERMANY

Here, inflationary dangers seem temporary and to a large extent offset by the austerity package and resulting tight fiscal policy. In addition wage restraint -- public sector unions have agreed an rise of just 1.3 percent in 1997 -- means monetary policy could be easier.
These factors and signs of slower money supply growth point to a further limited easing.
BRITAIN
Chancellor Kenneth Clarke has already raised rates a quarter of a point, although with the ruling Conservatives so far behind in opinion polls it had been thought he would to hold off.
The mainstream theory is that rates will have to rise again but some say higher rates are not a done deal.
Patrick Minford, one of the Treasury's advisors, believes Clarke was unwise. "I think it was quite a serious mistake," he said, adding that he thought the rise may have to be reversed.
CANADA

Canada is also getting close to the bottom of the rate cutting cycle but if growth remains weak rates will be cut. "Given the Bank of Canada's recent actions and statements there can be no guarantee they won't cut again if the opportunity presents itself," said David Coleman, chief economist at CIBC Wood Gundy.
REST OF G10
The picture for the rest of G10 is a little clearer. France, Italy, Belgium, Sweden and the Netherlands are all seen cutting further but for some this will depend on another German cut.

"Notwithstanding the efforts these countries have made to get their budget deficits down cutting rates is the tried and tested way of getting growth," said CIBC's Coleman. "And if you have tight fiscal policy you need the shock absorber of lower interest rates unless you want recession."
TOUGH TO CALL
"You have to think now about interest rate cycles with lower amplitude as part of the process of more stable and lower inflation," said Chase's Marshall.

In 1994 there was a huge overshoot when the markets became much too bearish about how far rates would go back up on the assumption that policy makers had got no better at reading economic cycles than they were in the late 1980s.
Because of the overestimate last time the markets are much less prepared to price in as much volatility.

"Barring shocks it looks as though cycles are going to smaller and therefore more difficult to call than in the good old days when we had 10 percent inflation and governments going for big blow-outs on budgets," Marshall said.
